4971.cfw: Srinivas 2010, the only first-hand study of Adilabad Gondi prosody, says the language has no overt stress, whereas Steever 1998 (a sketch drawn from Subrahmanyam 1968, which is itself does not discuss stress) and Krishnamurti 2003 (a statement about Dravidian as a whole) report non-phonemic initial-syllable stress; since every source denies contrastive stress and Srinivas puts the head of the word on the initial syllable, the disagreement is whether a weak initial prominence counts as stress at all.

4978.dq: Marichelle 1902: 6: 'parce-que la particule lu prenant l'accent tonique, peut-être considérée comme faisant partie du mot' (the accent is placed within the dictionary word, prefix + stem). By contrast the modern lengthening statement is phrasal: 'A single vowel is perceived long when it is in a penultimate syllable position of a phrase or sentence-final word' (Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008: 164).
4978.prule: No word-stress rule in the modern description: Civili is treated as a tone language (H/L tones, unmarked in the orthography) whose only positional prominence is vowel lengthening on the penultimate syllable of a phrase- or sentence-final word (Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008 Rule 5). The one stress statement is Marichelle 1902's 'accent tonique de pénultième', a word-level penultimate accent presupposed as a spelling rationale (prefix written together with a monosyllabic stem when it carries the accent: lu-to 'spoon', bi-gni 'faces', bi-ka 'beds').

4978.tone: Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008 (Stellenbosch PhD, Civili of Mayumba/Gabon) uses H/L tone throughout (abbreviations p. xxi; 'the marking of tones and other suprasegmental features at the orthographic level does not occur'), cites Blanchon 1990 for the tone inventory (Ndinga-Koumba-Binza & Roux 2009: 'consonants, vowels and tones': 'tones are not marked in Civili orthography'), and states no word-stress rule for Civili: stress appears only as a cross-linguistic factor in vowel duration (p. 133, Gussenhoven 2001 quote; p. 145 list of factors 'j. stress', p. 146 'd. tones') and in the phrase 'an unstressed nominal prefix syllable' (p. 30, citing Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2000) as a context for [a]-reduction. Penultimate prominence is described as phrase-level lengthening (p. 159: 'in a phrase- or sentence penultimate syllable the duration of the vowel is longer than in other positions'; p. 164 Rule 5, V -> [long] / __CV##; p. 146: long vowels 'only in the first syllable of disyllabic words or penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words'). Marichelle 1902 never mentions tone ('ton' occurs only as the French possessive; 'intonation' once s.v. Kunu-kuna); his 'accent tonique de pénultième' (31 'accent' hits, dozens of entries 'prend l'accent de (la) pénult.') is a dictionary convention for prefix + monosyllabic stem. The same author's grammar (Marichelle 1907, 'Accent tonique' pp. 10-11) states the rule explicitly, and it is initial in the word without its particle (which coincides with the penult only for disyllables such as 'Li mémé ... prononcez : mémé') rather than penultimate once the word has three or more syllables: 'La langue vilie a l'accent tonique. Les radicaux monosyllabes, à part de rares exceptions, laissent cet accent à leur particule ... Ex. ḳika, le lit. Ḳi est long, parce qu'il prend l'accent' (p. 10); 'Les mots de deux syllabes, ont l'accent sur la pénultième ... Les mots de trois syllabes, ont l'accent sur l'antépénultième, en général. Futika, plier, fu est long. Les mots de quatre syllabes ont, en général, l'accent sur la première syllabe, et parfois sur la troisième ... Quand un mot, un verbe spécialement, prend un suffixe, l'accent se reporte sur la première voyelle du radical. Sāla, sālila, sālilila. Est excepté le suffixe anga, qui prend l'accent ; sálilānga' (p. 11). Marichelle equates the accented syllable with length ('est long') and the 1907 chapter never mentions tone, so his 'accent' is the missionary perception of vowel length on the first syllable of the stem (on the prefix when the stem is monosyllabic), with the placement for monosyllabic stems reading as lexical tone; it is not a phrase-penultimate lengthening rule of the Ndinga-Koumba-Binza 2008 kind (p. 164 Rule 5), and its antepenultimate 'fu' in futika does not match Ndinga-Koumba-Binza's distribution of long vowels (p. 146: first syllable of disyllabic words or penultimate syllable of polysyllabic words).

tn.translation: If that is so, Ci-Vili nominals would have, for all themes of more than one syllable, only two types: Type I: H-H(L)n, Type II: H-L(L)n. Since the prefix is always high and the syllables after the theme-initial one always low, the only relevant classification criterion is the high or low tone of the radical syllable. In fact, if one keeps to citation forms, as Ndamba seems to do, all nominals divide neatly between these two types.

tn.quote: Vute has three tone levels, H, M, L, plus downstep. Vute has both lexical and grammatical tone. In the Vute (Vɨ́tè) orthography, H tone is written with an acute accent over the vowel/syllable nucleus, L tone is indicated with a grave accent over the vowel, the falling tones (HL or HM) are marked with a circumflex accent, M tone is unmarked as are the rising tones unless they occur on long vowels, when each vowel is marked with the corresponding tone. 4983.tone: Leenhardt's only prosodic remark on Wamoang is the lexical pitch pair le 'nous' (bas) vs le 'eux' (haut) under the template heading 'Accent et ton'; he does not call the language tonal, gives no other pitch-marked form, and says nothing about accent/stress. His general chapter (p. 11, line 48, verified by C) defers accent and tone to each language chapter: 'Il reste à connaître l'accent, le ton, et les particularités phonétiques de chaque langue. On en trouvera le détail au chapitre réservé à chacune de celles-ci.' The parallel §2 in the Pwapwa chapter is equally one pair ('neole = le nôtre: bas et sourd' / 'neole = le leur: haut et sonore'), so the heading is a fixed template whose content is whatever pitch pair he noted. Voegelin & Voegelin 1964: 63 (verified by C) restate the pair second-hand as 'Thirteen vowel symbols are used; vowels occur with at least two phonemic distinctions of tone.' Rivierre 1972 (BSLP 67: 302, verified by C) calls the cluster Waamwang belonged to 'les dialectes sans tons de Voh-Koné'. One pronoun pair from a 3-speaker questionnaire, unconfirmed by any later worker and contradicted by the specialist's classification of the sister dialects, does not establish a tone system; hence not determinable from the sources rather than tone or pitch accent.

4984.dq: Peter (1990: 115-117, 120-121) justifie cette analyse en expliquant que seulement quatre schèmes tonals – H, B, HB, BH – sont attestés sur les noms dissyllabiques simples, et qu’il n’existe pas de paires minimales tonales nominales opposant H contre ↑H (1). [tone is described on lexical words; no stress domain is described]
4984.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Waama is a two-tone language: contrastive H and B (low), with distinctive upstep (↑H) and downstep (↓B) partly due to floating low tones; the tone-bearing unit is the syllable (Peter 1990 analysed it as the moneme); lexical tone schemes on di-/trisyllabic nouns and verbs (HB, ↑HH, HH, BB, BH... on disyllabic nouns) are contrastive.

A ces tons sous-jacents s’associent des phénomènes de relèvement tonal et d’abaissement tonal dont les réalisations ↑H et ↓B respectivement assument une fonction distinctive (Peter 1990: 124, 195). 4984.tone: The whole report is about tone: two distinctive tones H and B (confirming Peter 1990 against the three-tone systems of the other Eastern Oti-Volta languages), distinctive upstep ↑H and downstep ↓B, floating B tones, TBU = syllable (§2.2, §3.2; Peter 1990's abstract says the moneme), tone schemes of disyllabic and trisyllabic nouns and verbs (§3.3-3.4), grammatical tone on pronouns and aspect markers. The word 'accent' occurs only for the orthographic grave/acute accent that writes tone on pronouns and particles; nothing anywhere on stress, intensity, prominence or an accented syllable, and no explicit denial of stress either. Cross-checks agree: Rowe 1991 p. 298 fn. 'There are two phonemic tones, high and low, but they are not written in the orthography'; Hartell 1993 alphabet page (image only) 'very high, high, low' tones; Eddyshaw 2024 §2.8.3 'Waama tonal data are scanty, and the sources differ'.

4986.prule: No positional rule: stress is contrastive (phonemic) and lexically specified. Any syllable of a word may carry stress, and a word may have none, one, several or all of its syllables stressed; minimal sets differ only in stress placement (/haáya/ 'wing' vs /háaya/ 'fuzz'; /mmáta/ 'a short way' vs /mmátá/ 'ground' vs /mmatáa/ 'spear'; /yeéna/ 'rope' vs /yéenna/ 'food').

4986.tone: The authors analyse the prosody as contrastive stress, not tone, but note that words with no or all syllables stressed 'may be identified by frame techniques as used in tone analysis' and cite Pike & Kindberg (1956, 'A problem in multiple stresses', on Campa) as a very similar system; word borders are marked by a pitch up-step (initial) and pitch down-drift (final). 4990.heavy: Syllable with a long vowel: 'All long vowels bear stress.' Vowel length is contrastive (§2.1.2, five vowels each with a long counterpart); at most one long vowel per word, restricted to the first or second syllable (§2.2.1; footnote 10 excepts inherently reduplicated words such as 'crow', 'pee-wee', 'nose bone', which carry two long vowels). 4990.prule: Primary stress falls on the long vowel if the word has one (a word has at most one long vowel, and it can stand only in the first or second syllable); otherwise primary stress falls on the first syllable. A second-syllable long vowel therefore takes primary stress and the first syllable is demoted to secondary (bìyá:yu 'two').
4990.srule: Secondary stress on the odd-numbered syllables after an initial primary, i.e. the 3rd (5th...) syllable (yánjaràn 'old woman'); when a second-syllable long vowel takes primary stress, the first syllable takes secondary stress (bìyá:yu 'two'). Placement after a second-syllable primary is not described.

4991.prule: Stress is predictable, not lexical, and is assigned on the written form of the word. Syllables are light (C)V or heavy (C)VV (surface closed syllables arise only from later vowel deletion and do not condition stress; they may be unstressed). Parse bimoraic (moraic-trochee) feet from the left edge of the word; the first syllable of each foot is stressed; primary stress goes to the leftmost foot.…
4991.srule: Secondary stress on the first syllable of each non-initial bimoraic foot (moraic trochees built from the left edge over the written form; a heavy (C)VV syllable is a foot by itself; an unfootable light syllable is unstressed): kwairanai (kwai)ra(nai) [ˈkpiːraˌneɪ], olisida (oli)(sida) [ˈɔliˌsid], soilidia (soi)(lidi)a [ˈsuːliˌdʒɪ], fafu'isinai (fafu)('isi)(nai) [ˈɸaɸˌʔisˌnaɪ], safitamiu (safi)ta(miu) [ˈsaɸtaˌmiʊ]; fasakwadola is parsed (fasa)kwa(dola) [ˈɸasak͡pɐˌdɔl]. 4992.tone: Two level tones H and L (sec. 5.5-5.6, p. 136); four lexical melodies H, L, HL (F), LH (R) contrasting on monosyllabic verbs and nouns, e.g. ʤu 'head' (n) vs ʤu 'steal' (v) (p. 136), lorɩ́ŋ 'hurry' vs lorɩ̀ 'untie' (p. 141-142); polysyllabic noun stems 'occur in the combination of all the melodies' (p. 142); TBU is the syllable, heavy and light syllables bear both simple and contour tones (sec. 5.3, p. 131); tonal processes include spreading and downstep/terracing whose limit 'is the entire utterance' (p. 156). The source says nothing at all about stress, accent, prominence, rhythm or intonation: a full-text search of the full finds 'stress' only in the gloss 'distress' (wordlist item 319), 'accent'/'promin' never, and the single 'foot' in sec. 3.5.2.2 ('A single vowel acting as a syllable most often serves as a pre-nuclear margin of the foot or serves as its final post-nuclear margin.', p. 72, p. 90) is an incidental phrase, not a prominence claim. Silence, not denial: the thesis neither asserts nor denies word stress.

4994.dq: L'accent tonique n'a pas seulement un rôle démarcatif au niveau du mot. Il sert aussi à marquer la "définitude". (Moyse-Faurie 2016 §1.3.2, p. 18; the word-level 'ordinary' accent of §1.3.1 is contrasted with the NP-level definitive accent.) Livingston 2016 p. 18: 'East Uvean has predictable stress on the penultimate mora of a word.'
4994.dloc: Moyse-Faurie 2016 §1.3.2 "L'accent dit de 'définitude'", p. 18 (printed; p. 19 of the HAL file); Livingston 2016 §2.3.3.4 'Assigning stress', p. 18.
4994.heavy: A syllable containing a long vowel ('une voyelle longue étant composée de deux mores', fn 5); Livingston 2016 p. 13 adds a final bimoraic vowel sequence [ˈCV,V] (consecutive vowels 'frequently pronounced as diphthongs'), and states that consonant codas are prohibited, so vowel length/bimoraicity is the only weight distinction.
4994.dflt: penultimate syllable (fále 'maison', maháki 'malade', alága 'cuisse'; katolíka, hahá'i in citation form)
4994.prule: Primary stress falls on the penultimate mora of the word: on the penultimate syllable when the final vowel is short (fále, maháki, alága), on the final syllable when its vowel is long, a long vowel counting as two morae with stress on its first mora (matapā́, falā́, fakapṓ). Livingston states the same rule and extends the bimoraic final to vowel sequences [ˈCV,V] (cf. Moyse-Faurie's peáu 'vague'); there are no codas (maximal syllable [CVː]/[CVV]). French loans conform: closed-syllable sources get an added final vowel and penultimate stress, open-syllable sources keep source-final stress through a long final vowel (kamiō, sinemā). A separate grammatical 'accent de définitude' shifts stress to the (lengthened) final vowel of the last word of a definite noun phrase.
4994.srule: Not mentioned in Moyse-Faurie 2016 (§1.3 'Accent et intonation', pp. 17-21, and loan accent p. 28, read in full). Livingston 2016 §2.3.2 (pp. 13-14): no secondary stress in words of three syllables or fewer; in words of four or more syllables a secondary stress tends to fall two morae before the primary-stressed mora, though it 'cannot currently be shown to have a fully predictable rule' (tapu'aki [ˌta.pu.ˈʔa.ki], pule-'aki [ˌpu.le-ˈʔa.ki], fe.ˌtau.ˈʔa.ki 'to fight').
4994.quote: L'accent tonique porte en général sur la pénultième sauf lorsque celle-ci comporte une voyelle longue⁵. Dans ce cas, l'accent tonique porte sur la dernière syllabe: fále "maison", tái "mer", 'átu "lancer"; maháki "malade", alága "cuisse", peáu "vague" mais matapā́ "porte", falā́ "argent", fakapṓ "assassiner". L'accent tonique ordinaire ne sera pas noté dans le reste de l'ouvrage; en effet, nous réservons le caractère graphique de l'accent aigu à la notation de l'accent tonique marquant la définitude. [footnote 5] De fait, il est plus exact de dire que l'accent porte toujours sur l'avant-derni…

4995.heavy: Primary stress is quantity-insensitive (root syllable). Secondary stress only: 'nur wenn die zweitletzte Silbe einen langen Vokal oder schwere Konsonanz enthält, wird sie betont' — a penult with a long vowel or heavy consonance takes the strongest secondary stress instead of the final syllable (a CVV+CVC-type condition, stated for the Nebenton only; not a QS coding of primary stress).
4995.prule: Main stress (Starkton) falls on the root syllable of native non-compound words, whatever the syllable count; prefixes are pretonic and unstressed (§ 23, p. 18: 'etwas größer ist der Stärkeunterschied zwischen der starkbetonten und der vorausgehenden Vortonsilbe, zB. in bitsiə beziehen, einholen; gitseiχt gezeigt; antwæg im Wege' — the page prints these three forms without stress marks; their prefix status follows from the prose). Nominal compounds carry main stress on the first member; place/field names and a few Adj+N compounds on the second. Loanwords are partly retracted to initial stress, but many (mostly recent) keep foreign late or final stress.
4995.srule: The strongest secondary stress (Nebenton) in words of three or more syllables mostly falls on the final syllable (Tǣ́rbinèr 'Visperterminer', fíɒrlinù); it falls on the penult instead only when the penult contains a long vowel or a heavy consonant cluster (ámeìsa 'Ameise', fịšterlòxti 'finstere').

4996.dq: the aim of this section is to demonstrate from an acoustic perspective that as a general pattern Walungge has second syllable stress, and not just second syllable high tone. (p. 192) ... synchronically tone is independent of stress in as much as the second syllable of a polysyllabic word has high tone regardless of whether the word has the prevailing second syllable stress pattern or whether the …
4996.dloc: Ch. 5, sec. 5.2.6 'Conclusion of acoustic analysis', thesis p. 209. Supporting: sec. 5.2.1 p. 192; sec. 5.2.2 p. 197; p. 202; sec. 5.2.5 p. 208; sec. 5.3.2 p. 211; sec. 5.6 p. 256
4996.heavy: Not applicable (quantity-insensitive). The source explicitly tests the case: 'In particular notice the case of when the first syllable is a heavy syllable (CVN), which because of its weight might be expected to attract stress. If the second syllable is a light syllable, whilst it does not have as long duration as the first syllable, it has longer duration than when the equivalent shape is a first syllable.' (p. 197), and concludes 'a general pattern of second syllable stress for all disyllabic non-verbs'.
4996.prule: Second-syllable stress on all polysyllabic non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, numerals), quantity-insensitive: a heavy CVN first syllable does not attract stress (p. 197), and the pattern holds for both H- and L-tone words. Verbs are stressed on the root, normally the first syllable; with the negative prefix the root (second syllable) is stressed (p. 208).
4996.srule: None: 'stress never occurs on the third or subsequent syllables' -- one stress per word (sigma-2 in non-verbs, the root = normally sigma-1 in verbs); the thesis never uses the term 'secondary stress' and reports no other prominence (stress section 5.2, pp. 192-209, read in full).

These differences cannot simply be explained as correlates of high tone because they occur on the second syllable even when both the first and second syllables have high tone. The conclusion is that as a general pattern Walungge has second syllable stress for words which are not ve…

4996.tone: Walungge is a word-tone language: a two-way H/L contrast, one underlying tone per word attached to the first mora of a disyllabic 'tonal foot' formed over the first two syllables regardless of their weight; the second syllable of every polysyllabic content word carries high pitch (e.g. sámba 'new' [44 44] vs sàmba 'bridge' [11 44]; órokpa 'toad' [44 44 21]; tɕémaladʑok 'butterfly' [44 44 21 11], p. 192); syllables after the second are unfooted and low. Monosyllables show a two-way pitch-melody contrast that also varies with syllable weight (p. 209). The author argues stress is diachronically the origin of the sigma-2 high tone but synchronically independent of it: the minority sigma-1-stressed nouns still have high pitch on sigma-2 (pp. 211, 256). Stress was established instrumentally (rhyme duration, F0 maximum, intensity; paired t-tests, disyllabic non-verbs, all CV/CVP/CVN shape combinations, both tones).

tn.quote: Underlyingly, Walungge has two phonologically contrastive tones, high (H) and low (L). The presence of a boundary tone, and the formation of a tonal foot for the purposes of attaching the tones to the tone bearing units, gives the rising, falling, and level pitch melodies that are transcribed above in the phonetic forms of words (see Chapter 5 for tonal analysis). ... 4997.prule: Word stress (relative prominence of a syllable by increased loudness) 'usually' falls on the root of verbs and deverbatives and on the initial syllable of nouns and other parts of speech (p. 56). The negative marker <a>, a lexical prefix present in every negated verb form, 'is the only prefix in Wambule' (p. 101) and never functions as the stressed syllable; in negated verbs stress 'generally' falls on the root following it, e.g. /AsicAm/ [e'sitsem] 'to not die' (p. 60). The grammar marks stress in phonetic transcription only where it is not on the initial syllable of the phonological word, 'especially in negated verbs', so the surface position is word-initial in most words and on the root (second syllable) in negated verbs. Described second-hand as a weak stress (Sampang chapter, citing Opgenort 2002: 60); unstressed syllables lose the vowel-length and /ya/~/e/, /wa/~/o/ contrasts.
